leads.subject: 1547 Iurghiceni property chain
leads.scope: Iurghiceni on the Bahlui, Hârlău district, Moldavia, 1547–1619
leads.next_action: Recover the full 1611 document text and the 1619 cotas 24–28 originals/transcriptions. Compare exact property descriptions, neighboring owners, witnesses, prior-title language and any ancestry statements. Search Iurghiceni records between 1547 and 1611 and after 1620 for an explicit link to Cican/Illea. Treat Frim/Frimu as a separate documented person until such a link is found.
leads.notes: Primary/archival catalog evidence confirms the 1547 charter (Cican/Cicican and son Illea) and a separate 1611 Iurghiceni testimony that Frim sold his ancestral holding. Published documentary indexes then identify 1619 Iurghiceni records: Costin and Lupu receive land bought from Milrica daughter of Udrea (27 May); Costin is empowered to possess Frimu's portion because he paid 46 talers for Frimu's ransom (27 May); and on 20 June Costin/Lupu receive Iurghiceni land bought from Iosif son of Vasile Cergas and a separate portion bought from Frimu son of Bilan. A 1620 record continues Costin's possession at Iurghiceni. None of these later records currently names Cican/Illea or proves descent from them.

leads.subject: Iurghiceni 1591–1599 ownership continuity
leads.scope: Iurghiceni continuity: 1591–1592 → 1611 → 1619
leads.next_action: Compare the full 1591–1592 and 1639 documents for Obrejie/Agafia/Agahia, priest Gavril, Băsărăbești-side property fractions, boundaries, witnesses and prior-title language. Search intervening 1592–1639 records for Obrejie, Agafia/Agahia and priest Gavril. If the property description and kinship language align, upgrade from research lead to probable identity continuity.
leads.notes: BNaR archival inventory establishes an Iurghiceni-specific sequence: 1591–1592 I/14, 1611 I/18, and later 1619 records. The 1599 I/15-a item is a separate court judgment and should not be treated as Iurghiceni ownership continuity merely because it is adjacent in the inventory. I/14 is especially useful: Ștefan son of Cătrîna, grandson of priest Gavril, sells his Iurghiceni share from the Băsărăbești side to his cousin Obrejie, son of Agafia and grandson of priest Gavril. The verso note 'Cost. Paladi hatm.' is a later archival annotation and must not be used to date the transaction. Major new continuity clue: DRH A XXV docs. 173 and 187 (15 and 22 July 1639) repeatedly identify Obrejie/Obreje, son of Agahia and nephew of priest Gavril, as acquiring Băsărăbești-family shares of Iurghiceni. The 1591–1592 BNaR record identifies Obrejie, son of Agafia and grandson of priest Gavril, as the cousin of Ștefan son of Cătrîna and buyer of the Băsărăbești-side Iurghiceni share. This is a strong candidate for the same person or the same family branch across 1591–1639, but identity is not yet proven; exact original spellings, ages/chronology and property descriptions must be compared.

leads.title: Cicicani / Ion of Cicicani — 1638 Hotin documentary cluster
leads.scope: Cicicani near Forosna in the historical Hotin region; 26 February 1638 record names Tațea, daughter of Ion from Cicicani, as Nasta's maternal grandmother and identifies inherited property in Cicicani.
evidence: DRH A. Moldova XXII, doc. 278, pp. 311–312, as cited by secondary historical studies
Historical settlement catalogues identify Cicicani near Forosna/Novoselița
leads.next_action: Recover and compare DRH A, vol. XXIV, doc. 249 (1638) and the 1643/1645 documents; determine whether earlier Cicicani records identify Ion or his descendants and whether any record independently uses Cican/Cicican as a personal surname. Keep this cluster separate from the 1547 Cican/Cicican at Iurghiceni unless an explicit documentary bridge is found.
leads.notes: The 26 February 1638 record is independently described in scholarly historical studies as Nasta, daughter of Ivan Vartic and Tațea, daughter of Ion din Cicicani, identifying Cicicani as a property-bearing locality in the historical Hotin region near Forosna/Novoselița. Later 1643 and 1645 records continue the same Cicicani property context through Nasta/Tațea's line. The wording supports a locative designation ('Ion din Cicicani') and property inheritance, not a Cican surname identification.

leads.subject: Cicănești / Cica / possible Cican toponymic-anthroponymic connection
leads.scope: Cicănești, Argeș, 1526–1565 and later
leads.notes: The official Cicănești local-history page confirms documentary attestation of the settlement on 11 June 1565. A secondary historical/onomastic source states that Cica is attested as a personal name in 1526 and discusses a proposed Cican-derived explanation for the place-name. This does not establish that the 1547 Moldavian Cican/Cicican or the user's family originated in Cicănești. Current BNaR inventory work also confirms the 1547 archival item exists in the national-library holdings; preserve this as provenance, not as a new occurrence. The 1547 BNaR primary charter is now independently verified through the National Library inventory: the original Slavonic document of 26 May 1547 confirms (Cican) and his son Illea over a share of Iurghiceni. The published DRH text renders the beneficiary as Cican in the entry but Cicican in the body. This is now the archive's earliest securely dated Cican/Cicican occurrence. It does not establish surname heredity or continuity to later Cicans.
leads.next_action: Recover the 1526 personal-name citation and the 1565 primary charter; determine the exact historical spelling and grammatical form of the place-name and personal name; search intervening and surrounding Wallachian records for Cica/Cican/Cicănești variants; compare chronology and geography without assuming identity or origin.

leads.subject: Iurghiceni 1611 Frim son of Bilan → Costinovici → 1619 Costin/Frimu property chain
leads.hypothesis: The 1611 sale by Frim son of Bilan to his nephew Costinovici may be connected to the Costin/Frimu property transactions documented in 1619 and later Iurghiceni records.
leads.notes: BNaR's 1611 inventory explicitly says Frim son of Bilan sold his Iurghiceni ocină to his nephew Costinovici. The 1619 BNaR inventory says Costin vistiernicul of Iurghiceni received an ocină purchased from Frimu son of Bălan for 46 silver talers; the 1620 document confirms Costin's Iurghiceni holding. A 1632 scholarly edition independently records Costin's Iurghiceni holding and local witnesses. These records strengthen the Costin/Frim documentary chain, but do not connect it to Cican/Cicican/Illea. A separate scholarly name index independently identifies Bilan as the father of Frim from Iurghiceni, citing the 1619 documentary volume. This supports treating the 1611 'Frim son of Bilan' and the 1619 'Frimu son of Bilan' as the same named father-son branch unless the original documents reveal otherwise. It still does not establish that Costinovici in 1611 is the later Costin vistiernic. The BNaR catalogue explicitly styles the 1611 nephew as 'Costinovici, vistier'. The 1619 documents style the later beneficiary 'Costin vistiernic' / 'Costin vistiernicel'. This makes the office/title comparison a concrete identity test, but the name-form difference remains unresolved. A closer reading of the 1619 edition reveals multiple Costin formulations: 'Costin and Lupu vistiernici' in the Iosif son of Vasile Cergas transaction, and 'Costin vistiernicel from Iurghiceni' in the Frimu son of Bilan transaction. Therefore the 1611 Costinovici identity cannot be solved by office/title alone; the exact person and transaction context must be compared. Critical clarification: the 6 January 1622 primary-edition record explicitly says 'Gligorie and his brother Costin, vistiernicei from Iurghiceni.' Thus Costin is demonstrably associated with a brother Gligorie by 1622. This is stronger than the earlier 1632 locality-only evidence and provides a key identity marker for the 1619 Costin. It still does not prove that the 1611 Costinovici is the same man. New caution: the 1632 record identifies a Gligorie at Iurghiceni as brother of Gavril, son of Palaghia and grandson of Miron. It does NOT call this Gligorie Costin's brother. The 1622 record calls Gligorie Costin's brother, but gives no parentage in the excerpt recovered. These could be the same Gligorie with different brothers, or different Gligories. Therefore the 1622→1632 Gligorie identification remains unresolved. Major new clue: the 1622 volume search results contain two closely paired 6 January entries concerning Costin from Iurghiceni and the same Rădeni/Umbrar acquisition context: one names 'Grigore and Costin vistiernicel', while doc. 129 names 'Gligorie and his brother Costin vistiernicei'. This strongly suggests Grigore/Gligorie is a documentary name-form variant for the same brother of Costin, although the original pages should still be checked before treating it as definitive. The 1632 sale says Gavril and Gligorie are sons of Palaghia/grandsons of Miron and that their share is selected from the shares of other brothers. Therefore the absence of Costin from that 1632 sale does not disprove that Costin could belong to the same wider sibling group. But no source currently names Costin as a son of Palaghia, so the connection remains unproven. BNaR's March 2025 digitized-document inventory adds two useful later finding aids: item 3357 records multiple Iurghiceni villagers attesting to Costin's holding; item 3444 records property shares of brothers Vasco, Costin and Iacob. Both are undated in the inventory, so they are leads only until the underlying scans are recovered. Correction: the Paladi name on BNaR item 3444 is an attribution/archival field whose chronological meaning is not yet established. A related caution is necessary because the genuine 1591–1592 Iurghiceni document I/14 also carries 'Cost. Paladi hatm.' on its verso. Therefore Paladi cannot by itself be used to date or exclude an Iurghiceni document. Item 3444 remains a separate undated finding aid until its underlying document is recovered.
leads.next_action: Recover the underlying item 3444 before assigning it to any century. Keep it separate from the 1611–1632 Costin identity chain until the document itself is dated. Focus the main chain on 1611, 1619, 1620, 1622 and 1632 primary records.

leads.subject: Iurghiceni Băsărăbești branch: Obrejie son of Agafia/Agahia, 1591–1639
leads.hypothesis: The Obrejie son of Agafia/Agahia and nephew/grandson of priest Gavril documented in 1591–1592 may be the same Obrejie who acquired Băsărăbești-family shares in Iurghiceni in 1639.
leads.notes: 1591–1592 BNaR record: Ștefan son of Cătrîna, grandson of priest Gavril, sells his Iurghiceni share from the Băsărăbești side to his cousin Obrejie, son of Agafia, grandson of priest Gavril. 1639 DRH A XXV docs. 173 and 187: Obrejie/Obreje, son of Agahia and nephew of priest Gavril, acquires Băsărăbești-side Iurghiceni shares. This is a strong continuity hypothesis but not yet a proven single-person identification. New identity-control result: the 26 May 1637 DRH A XXIII doc. 110 explicitly names two different Iurghiceni men called Obrejie—Obrejie son of Miron and Obrejie son of Lupu. Neither is identified as Obrejie son of Agahia/Agafia. This confirms that the name Obrejie alone is insufficient for merging the 1591–1592 and 1639 records and strengthens the need for patronymic/kinship/property matching. Further control point: a 28 November 1644 record identifies Miron of Iurghiceni as father of a deceased son Obrejie whose share was donated for his soul. This does not establish that this Obrejie was the 1639 son of Agahia; it is retained as a separate identity clue. The 1637 records likewise distinguish Obrejie son of Lupu and Obrejie son of Miron. The archive therefore treats the name Obrejie as a high-collision name at Iurghiceni. A further 31 March 1645 record names Obrejie and Miron of Iurghiceni together as local witnesses. Because no patronymic is supplied, this is a community/chronology marker only and does not prove that this Obrejie is the 1639 son of Agahia or the deceased son of Miron recorded in 1644. New negative-control evidence: DRH A XXIV doc. 410 (14 July 1638) contains another Agafia in the Iurghiceni title chain—Ion and Constantin, sons of Sidor and Agafia, associated with the Doșcești-side upper half of Iurghiceni. This demonstrates that Agafia/Agahia is also a recurring personal name in the locality and cannot be used alone to connect Obrejie to the 1591–1592 Băsărăbești branch.
leads.next_action: Compare the 1591–1592 Băsărăbești-side deed and 1639 Băsărăbești-side deeds at the property-title level. Treat Agafia/Agahia as a collision-prone given-name form and require patronymic, kinship, or property continuity before upgrading the Obrejie hypothesis.

leads.title: 1888–1889 Corcea school Cican/Cecan identity bridge
leads.hypothesis: The 1888–1889 Romanian school roll in Ghiorgea (Corcea) may contain the future Nicolae Cican and possibly the Dina Cican/Cecan documented in 1914–1915, but this must be tested through age, schooling, family and subsequent records.
leads.notes: External source check confirms the later Nicolae Cican timeline independently: Balamaci states he graduated from the Romanian high school in Bitola in 1901 and emigrated that year; the same study records him returning to Bitola for the Ottoman Romanian Congress on 10–11 July 1909 and returning again to Corcea in 1913. Burada's 1888–1889 Ghiorgea school list independently contains Nicola Cican. No source located in this pass provides age, parentage or another direct identifier connecting the 1888 Nicola Cican to the 1901 Nicolae Cican. Identity remains unresolved. Negative-control check: Burada's separate 1888–1889 Bitola primary-school list has 40 pupils and does not include Nicola Cican; his name occurs in the Ghiorgea school list. This is not evidence against the later 1901 Bitola high-school graduation claim because the records concern different schools/educational stages. It does, however, prevent merging the 1888 Ghiorgea pupil with an assumed 1888 Bitola pupil. New web-source reading of Balamaci's exact 1901 passage: he calls Nicolae '(Culicea) Cican' and describes him as a 'plisot' (Pleasa person) who graduated from the Romanian high school in Bitola in 1901 and emigrated that year. This is a meaningful geographic/community clue because the 1888 Ghiorgea school record is part of the Pleasa/Ghiorgea educational context. It remains circumstantial: the 1888 record does not state Pleasa as Nicola Cican's residence or parentage, and no direct bridge to the 1901 graduate has been recovered. Balamaci's wider context says roughly 160 young people from Pleasa were already in America by 1905 and specifically places Nicolae (Culicea) Cican in this Pleasa emigrant stream. This strengthens the community-level Pleasa connection, but it remains insufficient to identify the 1888 Ghiorgea schoolboy as the later Nicolae. Geographic negative-control: an independent academic study of an Aromanian congress lists N. Cican for Corița/Korçë and a separate T. Teja for Pleasa. This cautions against treating Balamaci's 'plisot' description as sufficient proof of Nicolae's place of origin or residence. Pleasa remains a community connection to investigate, not an established birthplace.

leads.title: Nicola / Nicolae / Nicolae (Culicea) Cican name-form reconciliation
leads.hypothesis: The forms Nicola Cican, Nicolae Cican and Nicolae (Culicea) Cican may represent the same historical person, but the archive must establish the naming conventions and source context before treating them as equivalent.
leads.notes: Current source-registry audit: Burada's 1888 school roll uses 'Nicola Cican'; the 1915 contemporary first-person document uses 'Nicola Cican'; Farsharotu's historical page uses 'Nicolae Cican'; Balamaci's secondary study uses 'Nicolae (Culicea) Cican'. 'Culicea' currently appears only in the secondary Balamaci source in the registry. Therefore it must be treated as an unexplained biographical identifier, not as evidence linking the 1888 and later records. Next step: locate the original/earlier source behind the Culicea form or another contemporary document using it. Balamaci's original 1901 passage itself—not merely a later summary—uses 'Nicolae (Culicea) Cican' and calls him a 'plisot', i.e. associated with Pleasa. This gives 'Culicea' a contemporary-source context and makes Pleasa a priority for the identity investigation, but it still does not explain whether Culicea is a byname or other identifier. New contextual evidence: Dumitru Carabaș's Aromanian personal-name reference lists 'Culicea' under the Nicolae name group ('Culícea, PM, NF, v. Nicolae'). This supports the possibility that 'Culicea' is a Nicolae-derived personal/byname form rather than a separate surname, but the source is general onomastics and does not identify Nicolae Cican specifically. Therefore it is contextual evidence only.

leads.title: 1547 Cican/Cicican name-function and Illea family bridge
leads.hypothesis: The 1547 Cican/Cicican and his son Illea may leave further documentary traces in Iurghiceni or neighboring Moldavian records, potentially clarifying whether Cican/Cicican functioned as a personal name, hereditary surname, patronymic or byname.
leads.notes: The 1547 charter names Cican/Cicican and son Illea and confirms a property share in Iurghiceni. The 1591–1592 Iurghiceni chain begins a later Băsărăbești branch but currently provides no proven link to the 1547 family. Priority is to search 1547–1590 records for Illea, Cican/Cicican variants, the same property fraction/boundaries, and related witnesses. Do not infer hereditary surname continuity from the 1547 occurrence alone. First continuity search across the available indexed 1547–1590 material did not recover a defensible later occurrence of Illea or Cican/Cicican tied to the same Iurghiceni property share. BNaR inventory confirms I/5 (1547) is followed by I/6 (1558), while the next clearly Iurghiceni-specific BNaR item in this series is I/14 (1591–1592); no continuity bridge was established. The 1547 charter itself is explicit that Cican/Cicican and Illea paid 60 Tatar zlotys for one-fifth of one-quarter of Iurghiceni. This failed bridge is recorded as a negative research result. BNaR's official inventory now provides a concrete intervening sequence: I/5 (1547 Cican + son), I/6 (1558 Bahlui property to Giurgea and relatives), I/10 (1575 Iurghiceni property to Burlan and Nikita, sons of Drăgan), then I/14 (1591–1592 Iurghiceni share sale). The intervening inventory entries do not name Cican/Cicican, so no continuity is inferred. The 1547 DRH text precisely identifies the purchased fraction as one-fifth of one-quarter of Iurghiceni and names son Ilca/Illea. Property-boundary comparison remains the next possible bridge. New DRH A VII evidence shows the 2 Aug 1575 Iurghiceni entries concern Drăghici son of Sofrin's property: Condrea receives a part, and Burlan/Nichita receive half of Drăghici's part. No Cican/Cicican or Illea appears in these entries. This is a useful negative control, not a continuity claim. Pre-1547 search audit completed against indexed BNaR/DRH material. BNaR's immediately preceding 1498 item is a Milcinești boundary record, not a Cican occurrence. Searches combining Cican/Cicican with Iurghiceni and earlier Moldavian material produced no defensible earlier attestation. This is a search result, not proof of absence. New high-value archival target identified: BNaR I/227–I/231 (1673) includes an undated list of Iurghiceni estate documents, a list of 19 purchase deeds (only first dated), a village situation, and share/boundary lists explicitly derived from purchase deeds. The underlying material may preserve older deeds relevant to reconstructing the 1547 share, but Cican/Illea continuity is not yet established. Major bridge found: DRH A XXVII records a 22 July 1643 order from Vasile Lupu requiring inhabitants of Iurghiceni and Tălhărești to bring 'all old documents' to a boundary investigation of parts of those villages. This proves older Iurghiceni title documents were actively relevant in 1643. It does not identify Cican, but it strengthens the strategy of tracing the 1547 share through surviving/recorded older deeds rather than relying on surname matches.
